name: Returning Home
description: Yura has been walking for some time already and is planning to return home. He needs to get home as fast as possible. To do this, Yura can use the instant-movement locations around the city. Let's represent the city as an area of $$$n \times n$$$ square blocks. Yura needs to move from the block with coordinates $$$(s_x,s_y)$$$ to the block with coordinates $$$(f_x,f_y)$$$. In one minute Yura can move to any neighboring by side block; in other words, he can move in four directions. Also, there are $$$m$$$ instant-movement locations in the city. Their coordinates are known to you and Yura. Yura can move to an instant-movement location in no time if he is located in a block with the same coordinate $$$x$$$ or with the same coordinate $$$y$$$ as the location. Help Yura to find the smallest time needed to get home.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ — the size of the city and the number of instant-movement locations ($$$1 \le n \le 10^9$$$, $$$0 \le m \le 10^5$$$). The next line contains four integers $$$s_x$$$ $$$s_y$$$ $$$f_x$$$ $$$f_y$$$ — the coordinates of Yura's initial position and the coordinates of his home ($$$ 1 \le s_x, s_y, f_x, f_y \le n$$$). Each of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains two integers $$$x_i$$$ $$$y_i$$$ — coordinates of the $$$i$$$-th instant-movement location ($$$1 \le x_i, y_i \le n$$$).
output_specification: In the only line print the minimum time required to get home.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1422D — Returning Home [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
